subtype: Steady adult for a frightened child [Response]
passage: At the children's home in Darjeeling, Chandrika rang the little brass bell at seven every morning, the same three rings. For the first weeks, Dolma, five, hid under the bunk whenever voices rose, even happy ones. Chandrika never pulled her out. She sat on the floor and said, "Breakfast is paratha today. I'll save yours." One day Chandrika snapped at a boy for spilling milk, and Dolma froze. Later Chandrika knelt beside her. "I was too loud. That wasn't okay. I'm sorry." By the fourth month, Dolma was waiting at the door at seven, holding the bell out for her.

qa.q: How many times did Chandrika ring the bell each morning?
qa.a: She rang it three times, the same three rings each morning.

qa.q: Why might Dolma hide under the bunk when voices rose?
qa.a: Raised voices seemed to feel dangerous to her, even happy ones, so she hid to feel safe.

qa.q: What did Chandrika do after snapping at the boy, and why did it matter?
qa.a: She knelt by Dolma, admitted she was too loud and said sorry, which repaired the moment and showed an adult can mend a mistake.

qa.q: What would change if Chandrika had pulled Dolma out from under the bunk?
qa.a: Dolma would likely feel more frightened and learn that adults force things, which would slow her trust.

grounding: A carer at a children's home offers the same routine, a calm tone and repair after a sharp moment, and over months a frightened child comes to trust her.

subtype: Steady adult for a frightened child [Response]
passage: Our neighbour Francis started fostering Ira last spring. She was five and flinched at everything, even his laugh. I've watched them from my balcony for months. Every evening at six he waters the tulsi pot, and she sits on the step with her doll. Same time, same step. Once she threw her plate, and he didn't shout. He said, "Plates break. You're safe. Let's sweep together." Some days she still backs away from him. But last week I saw her take his hand to cross the lane without checking his face first. I don't know what's in her head. It just looked like trust.

qa.q: What does Francis water every evening at six?
What might Ira be feeling when she takes Francis's hand without checking his face first?
qa.a: She seems to feel safe enough with him now, trusting him without watching for danger.

qa.q: What choice did Francis make when Ira threw her plate, and why did it help?
qa.a: He stayed calm, told her she was safe and invited her to sweep together, which showed her an adult who does not explode.

qa.q: How might Francis feel on the days Ira still backs away?
qa.a: He may feel sad, but he keeps the routine steady, as if he knows trust takes months.

grounding: A neighbour watches a foster father's predictable routine and calm response to an outburst slowly help a frightened five-year-old trust him.
